title: 1.58-bit LLMs: ternary weights, BitLinear and bitnet.cpp
summary: Why BitNet b1.58 uses weights in {-1, 0, +1}: absmean quantization, matmuls of additions, STE training, the scaling evidence, packed CPU and GPU kernels, and a tiny BitNet you train and pack yourself.
outcomes: Explain why a ternary weight carries log2(3) = 1.58 bits and why the zero value matters
Compute absmean ternary weights and absmax INT8 activations for a small matrix and vector
Trace a ternary matrix-vector product as integer adds and subtracts with one rescale per output
Explain why training from scratch with latent weights and STE beats post-training quantization
Weigh the scaling evidence for ternary models (b1.58, Spectra, ParetoQ, precision scaling laws) and its limits
Describe the full 2B4T recipe and how BitNet v2 and BitNet Distillation extend it
Compute packed memory for a 2B ternary model and explain how I2_S, TL1, TL2 and the W2A8 GPU kernel work
Train a tiny BitNet, pack it into 2-bit bytes and verify an integer kernel against the PyTorch forward

lessons.title: Why weight bytes set the price of decoding

blocks.md: In GPU and inference basics you saw that decoding one token reads every weight once, so the time per token has a floor of *weight bytes / memory bandwidth*. Weights are the bill. Take BitNet b1.58 2B4T, the model this course is built around. The name reads in two parts: b1.58 for weights that are each -1, 0 or +1, about 1.58 bits apiece, and 2B4T for about 2 billion parameters trained on 4 trillion tokens. Its config (hidden size 2560, FFN size 6912, 30 layers, 5 KV heads of size 128) gives **2,084,044,800** weights inside linear layers, plus a 128,256 x 2560 embedding.

Here is where that count comes from. Each layer has four attention projections. Queries and outputs are 2560 x 2560 each, while keys and values are only 2560 x 640, because the 20 query heads share 5 key-value heads of 128 numbers (grouped-query attention, from GPU and inference basics). That is 16,384,000 weights. The feed-forward network has three matrices (gate, up and down) of 2560 x 6912 weights each: 53,084,160. One layer holds 69,468,160, and 30 layers hold 2,084,044,800.

The embedding is separate: one row of 2560 numbers for each of the 128,256 tokens in the vocabulary. It stays in **bfloat16**, short for brain floating point, a format from Google Brain: 16 bits like FP16, but with FP32's 8 exponent bits and only 7 mantissa bits, so it keeps FP32's range with less precision. 2B4T **ties** its output head to this matrix: the same rows turn the last hidden vector into a score for every vocabulary token, so it is read on every decoded token.

Stored as FP16 (2 bytes each), those linear weights are **4.17 GB**. At 1.58 bits each (the information in a value that can be one of three; lesson 2 derives it) they would be **0.41 GB**. Since decode speed is roughly bandwidth divided by bytes read, cutting bits per weight raises the ceiling on tokens per second almost proportionally. Drag the bandwidth slider in the plot below to see the ceiling for a laptop (around 100 GB/s) versus a server GPU.

blocks.title: Decode ceiling vs bits per weight (2.08B linear weights)

scenes.caption: Simplified model: tokens/s = bandwidth / bytes read per token, ignoring KV cache, activations and compute. At 100 GB/s, FP16 weights cap decode near 24 tokens/s.
Ternary weights at 1.585 bits raise the same ceiling to about 242 tokens/s, roughly 10x, because every token reads 10x fewer bytes.
The catch: a 128,256 x 2560 output head kept in BF16 is 0.66 GB, more than all the ternary weights. With it the ceiling at 1.585 bits drops to about 93 tokens/s.
More bandwidth lifts every curve equally. The ratio between formats, not the absolute number, is what bits per weight buys.
Add the KV cache at 4,096 tokens of context: 0.31 GB more per token. The ternary ceiling falls from about 93 to 72 tokens/s, and its lead over FP16 shrinks from 4.5x to 3.7x.

blocks.md:
Weights are not the only bytes a decode step reads. Each new token also reads the **KV cache**, the keys and values stored for every earlier token (GPU and inference basics). For 2B4T at 2 bytes per value that is 2 (keys and values) x 30 layers x 5 KV heads x 128 numbers x 2 bytes = **76,800 bytes per token of context**. At 1,024 tokens of context a decode step reads 0.08 GB of cache; at 4,096 tokens, the model's maximum, 0.31 GB, close to the 0.41 GB of ternary weights.

Ternary weights do nothing to those bytes, so the longer the context, the smaller the speedup. The last scene of the plot adds them (drag the context slider).

The usual way to shrink weights is **post-training quantization (PTQ)**: train in full precision, then round the finished weights to fewer bits, sometimes with clever error correction (GPTQ, AWQ, QuIP). **GPTQ** (named for generative pre-trained transformer quantization) rounds one weight column at a time and nudges the weights not yet rounded to cancel the error, using second-order statistics of the layer's inputs. **AWQ** (activation-aware weight quantization) scales up the few weight channels that meet large activations, so rounding hurts them less. **QuIP** (quantization with incoherence processing) first multiplies the weights by random orthogonal matrices, so no single weight is an outlier. PTQ works well at 8 and 4 bits. Below that it falls apart.

Two terms for the experiment below. **Perplexity** is e raised to the average negative log-likelihood per token, which is the training loss: it reads as the number of equally likely next tokens the model is torn between, so lower is better and a perfect model scores 1. **Absmax quantization** sets the scale so the largest absolute value in the tensor lands on the top of the integer grid, then rounds every value to that grid; lesson 3 uses it for activations.

blocks.prompt: The BitNet paper (Wang et al., 2023) applied PTQ methods to a 6.7B FP16 Transformer at 8, 4, 2 and 1 bits. Guess the validation perplexity (lower is better; the FP16 model scores 15.19) after rounding its weights to 1 bit with absmax quantization.
blocks.reveal: **3.5 x 10^23.** The model is destroyed. GPTQ at 2 bits reached 1032 and QuIP at 2 bits 70.43. Meanwhile **BitNet**, a model trained from scratch with 1-bit weights and 8-bit activations, scored **17.07**, close to the FP16 model's 15.19.

blocks.md: The chart scores the same 6.7B models on four multiple-choice commonsense tests, **zero-shot**: the model sees no solved examples in its prompt. HellaSwag asks for the sensible ending of a described scene (4 choices); Winograd and Winogrande ask which noun a pronoun refers to (2 choices); StoryCloze asks for the right ending of a short story (2 choices). Random guessing scores 25, 50, 50 and 50 percent, which averages to 43.75, the 43.8 floor in the chart.

blocks.title: 6.7B models: average zero-shot accuracy (BitNet paper, Table 3)

scenes.caption: Reference points: random guessing averages 43.8 on these four tasks; the FP16 Transformer reaches 57.8.
Post-training quantization degrades smoothly at first (56.7 at 8 bits, 52.9 at 4 bits) then collapses: 49.0 at 2 bits and 44.6 at 1 bit, barely above random.
BitNet, trained with 1-bit weights from the start, scores 55.9. Same bit budget as the collapsed PTQ model, a completely different outcome.

blocks.md:
That gap is the whole idea of this course. Instead of compressing a model that was optimized for real-valued weights, **train the model with low-bit weights from the first step**, so the optimizer finds a solution that works inside the constraint. The line of work comes from Microsoft Research:

- **BitNet** (Oct 2023): binary weights in {-1, +1}, 8-bit activations, trained from scratch up to 30B parameters.
- **BitNet b1.58** (Feb 2024): ternary weights in {-1, 0, +1}; reported to match an FP16 LLaMA-style model (the architecture of Meta's open LLaMA models, the standard recipe for open large language models) of the same size and tokens from 3B parameters up.
- **BitNet b1.58 2B4T** (Apr 2025): the first open native 1-bit LLM at 2B scale, 4 trillion training tokens, with GPU and CPU kernels (**bitnet.cpp**, Microsoft's CPU inference program, covered in lesson 7).
A 1.58-bit model is not a compressed full-precision model. It is a model whose weights were ternary during training, so nothing is lost when you ship the ternary weights.

blocks.question: Decode on a laptop is memory-bandwidth-bound. Which change gives the biggest speedup ceiling for the same model?
options: Storing weights in 2 bits instead of 16
Switching attention to a faster softmax implementation
Doubling the number of CPU cores used for the matmuls
Using FP32 accumulators instead of FP16
blocks.explain: When decode is bandwidth-bound, time per token is about bytes read divided by bandwidth. Going from 16 to 2 bits reads 8x fewer weight bytes. More cores help only when compute is the bottleneck, and softmax or accumulator changes do not reduce weight traffic.

blocks.question: Why does post-training quantization to 1 bit fail so badly while BitNet at 1 bit nearly matches FP16?
options: PTQ uses worse rounding rules than BitNet
BitNet keeps a hidden FP16 copy of the weights at inference
BitNet uses more parameters than the PTQ baseline
PTQ rounds weights that were optimized for real values; BitNet's optimizer chose weights that already work as 1-bit values
blocks.explain: The BitNet team's FAQ puts it directly: PTQ can only quantize weights around the full-precision values, which need not be where good low-precision solutions lie. Training with the quantizer in the loop lets the optimizer search among ternary solutions. At inference BitNet uses only the low-bit weights, and the compared models have the same size.

lessons.title: Ternary weights: log2(3), absmean and the power of zero

blocks.md: A weight that can take 3 values, each equally likely, carries $\log_2 3$ bits of information, because $k$ equally likely choices need $\log_2 k$ bits to name. Two bits name 4 things, one bit names 2, and 3 sits in between. That is where the name **b1.58** comes from.

blocks.caption: Five ternary weights have 243 combinations, which fit in one byte: 8/5 = 1.6 bits per weight, close to the 1.585 limit. Real kernels trade some of that density for simpler unpacking, as lesson 7 shows.

blocks.md: BitNet b1.58 turns a real-valued matrix $W$ (n x m) into ternary values with **absmean quantization**: divide by the mean absolute value $\gamma$, then round and clip to {-1, 0, +1}. A tiny $\epsilon$ avoids division by zero.

blocks.caption: RoundClip rounds to the nearest integer, then clamps the result into the range -1 to 1. The scale is one number per weight matrix (per tensor). The effective weight is gamma times the ternary value.

blocks.md: Let us run it on a toy 4 x 4 matrix. The 16 absolute values sum to 4.59, so $\gamma = 4.59 / 16 = 0.286875$. Anything with $|W/\gamma| < 0.5$ rounds to 0, which here means $|W| < 0.143$.

blocks.title: Absmean quantization of a toy 4 x 4 weight matrix

scenes.caption: Real-valued weights W. Mean absolute value gamma = 0.286875. Small entries like -0.07 and 0.03 carry little signal.
Divide by gamma. Now the threshold for keeping a weight is 0.5 in magnitude. Entries like 3.07 and -2.13 are far outside [-1, 1] and will be clipped.
Six entries have |W/gamma| below 0.5: -0.24, 0.10, 0.38, 0.17, -0.07 and 0.31. They will round to 0, switching off 6 of 16 weights.
RoundClip result: 6 zeros, 6 plus ones, 4 minus ones. Note 3.07 and 1.46 both became +1: 1.46 by rounding, 3.07 by clipping. Only sign and on/off survive.
Dequantized view gamma x ternary: every weight is now -0.287, 0 or +0.287. Mean absolute error versus W is 0.146, about half of gamma. A trained BitNet never sees W; it only ever used this version.

blocks.md:
If you know per-channel post-training quantization, one gamma for a whole matrix looks far too coarse: rows full of large weights and rows full of small ones share one step size. For rounding a finished matrix it would be. Two things make it work in BitNet (the papers do not analyze this; this is what the code does):

- **The scale is inside training.** The optimizer only ever sees gamma times ternary values, so it settles on latent weights for which one shared step works, instead of a matrix that must be approximated afterwards.
- **Each input channel is scaled before the matrix.** Every BitLinear normalizes its input first (lesson 3), and RMSNorm's learned gain multiplies each input channel by its own number, which is the same as giving each column of $W$ its own scale.

One gamma per *logical* matrix is the rule: the released 2B4T GPU converter keeps separate gammas for the query, key and value matrices even where it stores them fused.

blocks.prompt: In a trained BitNet b1.58 checkpoint, what fraction of weights do you expect to be 0?
blocks.reveal: The team's FAQ reports the distribution of {-1, 0, +1} in checkpoints is **nearly uniform**, so roughly a third are zero, set by the absmean formula. They note you could raise the share of zeros by scaling gamma up, but preliminary experiments showed that hurt performance.

blocks.md: Why add 0 at all? The original BitNet used binary weights: $\widetilde{W} = \mathrm{Sign}(W - \alpha)$ with $\alpha$ the mean of $W$. Subtracting $\alpha$ centers the weights on zero, so roughly half land on each side, and a scale $\beta$, the mean absolute value of $W$, restores their size. Every input always pushes every output up or down. With a zero, a weight can ignore an input entirely, which the b1.58 paper calls **explicit feature filtering** and credits for stronger modeling. The FAQ adds what else was tried: {-1, +1} scaled well but was weaker, especially at small sizes; {0, 1} was unstable and diverged early; 5 levels {-2, ..., 2} were unnecessary since ternary already matched full precision.

"1-bit LLM" is the family name, not the bit count. BitNet b1.58 weights are ternary (about 1.58 bits), the original BitNet was binary (1 bit), and in both the activations are 8-bit and the embeddings stay in higher precision.

Why the mean and not the max? An absmax scale would be set by the single largest weight, so most weights would fall below half of it and round to 0. The mean tracks the typical weight, giving a useful mix of zeros and plus or minus ones.

blocks.question: A weight matrix has gamma = 0.4. Which ternary values do the weights [0.5, -0.1, -0.9, 0.19] get?
blocks.explain: Divide by gamma: [1.25, -0.25, -2.25, 0.475]. Round: [1, 0, -2, 0], then clip -2 to -1. Note 0.475 is just under the 0.5 threshold, so 0.19 is switched off even though it is not tiny.

blocks.question: You pack 5 ternary weights per byte. How many bits per weight is that, and how far is it from the information limit?
options: 1.6 bits, about 0.015 bits above log2(3)
1.58 bits, exactly the limit
2 bits, since each weight needs a 2-bit code
1.67 bits, because 3 weights need 5 bits
blocks.explain: 3^5 = 243 fits in 256 codes, so 8 bits hold 5 weights: 8/5 = 1.6 bits each, versus log2(3) = 1.585. 2 bits is what simple per-weight codes use, and 1.67 (5 bits per 3 weights) is bitnet.cpp's TL2 layout (lesson 7), which trades density for fast lookups.

lessons.title: BitLinear: a matrix multiply made of additions

blocks.md: BitNet replaces every `nn.Linear` (PyTorch's ordinary fully connected layer) in attention and the FFN with a **BitLinear** layer. Inside it, weights are ternary and activations are 8-bit integers (W1.58A8, read as weights at 1.58 bits, activations at 8 bits). Activations are quantized with **absmax** per token: scale the vector so its largest magnitude maps to 127, the largest value a signed 8-bit integer holds (its range is -128 to 127), then round. This is the official training code's formula.

blocks.caption: In words: s stretches the token so its largest entry is 127, x_q is that vector rounded to integers, and the output is the integer product times gamma over s. Both scales sit outside the integer product, so they are applied once per output, not once per weight.

blocks.md: Before quantizing, BitLinear normalizes its input. The original BitNet used **SubLN** (sub-layer normalization, from the Foundation Transformers paper): a LayerNorm placed right before each quantized linear layer, so the variance of its output stays near 1, as in a full-precision layer. The official code uses **RMSNorm**, a cheaper LayerNorm that skips subtracting the mean: it divides the vector by the root mean square of its entries, then multiplies by a learned gain.

blocks.title: Inside BitLinear at inference

scenes.caption: Activations arrive in BF16. A normalization (SubLN; RMSNorm in the official code) keeps their variance stable, which the BitNet paper adds specifically so quantized outputs keep a sane scale.
Each token's vector is scaled so its max magnitude is 127 and rounded to INT8. The scale s is kept for later.
The core: ternary weights times INT8 activations. Every product is +v, -v or nothing, so the inner loop is integer additions and subtractions.
One multiply per output undoes both scales: y = (gamma / s) x integer sum. Apart from the normalization and the absmax step, that is the only floating-point arithmetic in the layer.

blocks.md: Now a concrete pass. Use the ternary matrix from lesson 2 (gamma = 0.286875) and the activation vector x = [1.31, -0.4, 2.6, 0.7]. The max magnitude is 2.6, so s = 127 / 2.6 = 48.846.

blocks.title: Absmax INT8 quantization of one token

scenes.caption: The token's activations. The largest magnitude, 2.6 at index 2, sets the scale.
Multiply by s = 48.846. The max lands exactly on 127; the rest scale proportionally.
Round to integers. Worst rounding error here is 0.46 of one step out of 127, under 0.4% of the range.

blocks.title: Ternary matrix-vector product with no multiplies
blocks.code:
W = [[ 1, 0, 1,-1],
     [ 0, 1,-1, 0],
     [-1, 0, 1, 0],
     [ 1,-1, 1, 0]]      # ternary weights
xq = [64, -20, 127, 34]  # int8 activations
gamma, s = 0.286875, 48.846
y = []
for row in W:
    acc = 0                  # integer accumulator
    for w, v in zip(row, xq):
        if w == 1:
            acc += v
        elif w == -1:
            acc -= v
        # w == 0: skip, no work
    y.append(acc * gamma / s)  # one multiply per output

scenes.caption: Row 0 of W is [1, 0, 1, -1]. Start an integer accumulator at 0.
Weight +1 times 64: just add 64.
Weight 0: skip the input entirely. This is the feature filtering the zero buys.
Weight +1 times 127: add.
Weight -1 times 34: subtract. Row 0's integer sum is 157, from two adds and one subtract.
The other rows the same way: -20 - 127 = -147, -64 + 127 = 63, 64 + 20 + 127 = 211. 10 add or subtract steps in total, 4 multiplies.

blocks.prompt: The full-precision answer W x with the original real weights is [0.541, -0.990, 0.040, 2.164]. The ternary result is [0.922, -0.863, 0.370, 1.239]. Which step caused most of the gap: INT8 activations or ternary weights?
blocks.reveal: **Ternary weights.** Using the ternary W with the unquantized x gives [0.921, -0.861, 0.370, 1.236], almost identical to the INT8 result, so the 8-bit activations cost almost nothing. The large error comes from rounding a matrix that was never trained to be ternary. That is post-training quantization in miniature. A trained BitNet has no such gap because its real-valued weights never existed at inference: the network learned to compute with the ternary ones.

blocks.md: Why does avoiding multiplies matter? Using the energy model the BitNet papers cite (Horowitz, ISSCC 2014, with 7 nm figures via Zhang et al., 2022), at a 7 nm process an FP16 multiply costs 0.34 pJ and an FP16 add 0.16 pJ, while an INT8 add costs 0.007 pJ. A pJ is a picojoule, 10^-12 joules; ISSCC is the International Solid-State Circuits Conference, where Horowitz tabulated energy per operation; 7 nm names a chip manufacturing generation, and smaller generations spend less energy per operation. One FP16 multiply-accumulate is 0.50 pJ against 0.007 pJ for the ternary add: a ratio of **71.4x**, which is the figure the b1.58 paper reports for matmul arithmetic energy.

blocks.title: Arithmetic energy per operation at 7 nm (pJ)

scenes.caption: An FP16 weight times an activation needs a multiply (0.34 pJ) and an add into the running sum (0.16 pJ).

A ternary weight needs only an INT8 add or subtract: 0.007 pJ, a sliver on this scale. 0.50 / 0.007 = 71.4x. This is arithmetic only; it ignores the energy of moving data, which shrinks too but separately.

blocks.md: "Matmul becomes additions" applies to the weight matrices. Attention scores (queries Q times keys K, then the attention weights times values V) multiply activations by activations, so they are not ternary. And the speedup only appears with a kernel that actually exploits ternary weights, which lesson 7 covers.

**Scale granularity.** BitNet picks the coarsest scales there are: one gamma per weight matrix and one s per token. Weight-only quantization of ordinary models usually goes finer, with one scale per output row (per-channel) or per group of, say, 128 weights (per-group, as in the group-wise INT4 used with GPTQ and AWQ). More scales lower the rounding error of a fixed matrix, but each group's partial sum then needs its own multiply: a row of k weights in groups of g costs k / g multiplies instead of one. And unless training used the same groups, inference no longer computes what the model learned with, the mismatch behind lesson 7's lossless test.

Why activations stay at 8 bits: per-token absmax gives the largest entry 127 levels, so a few outliers still leave room for the rest. At 4 bits (-8 to 7) one outlier squeezes most entries to 0. The BitNet team found the states before the FFN down projection the worst. BitNet a4.8 keeps those at 8 bits and sparsifies them; BitNet v2 rotates them with a Hadamard transform first (lesson 6).

blocks.question: A ternary weight row has 1000 entries, 350 of them zero. Roughly what arithmetic does one output need?
options: 1000 multiplies and 999 adds
350 integer adds and 650 multiplies
650 multiplies, since zeros are skipped
650 integer adds or subtracts, then 1 multiply by the combined scale
blocks.explain: Each +1 adds the activation, each -1 subtracts it, each 0 is skipped: about 650 integer add or subtract steps. The scales gamma and s are shared, so they are applied once to the final sum.

blocks.question: A teammate implements BitLinear by computing gamma / s and multiplying it into every activation before the ternary matmul. What is wrong?
options: It double-counts gamma
It changes the result because gamma is per row
Nothing, it is mathematically identical and just as fast
The activations become non-integer, so the inner loop needs floating-point arithmetic again, losing the INT8 add advantage
blocks.explain: Scales are pulled outside the sum so the inner loop stays on small integers. Pre-multiplying makes every activation a float, so the adds become float adds. The math is equal in exact arithmetic, but the efficiency argument disappears. The official inference code applies both scales after the low-bit GEMM.

lessons.title: Training from scratch: latent weights and the STE

blocks.md: Training with ternary weights has an obvious problem. RoundClip is a staircase: flat almost everywhere, with jumps. Its derivative is 0 wherever it exists, so backpropagation through it would send zero gradient to every weight and nothing would learn.

The fix BitNet uses is the **straight-through estimator (STE)**, studied by Bengio, Leonard and Courville (2013), the reference BitNet cites: use the quantizer in the forward pass, but in the backward pass pretend it was the identity and pass the gradient straight through. To have something to pass it to, training keeps a full-precision **latent weight** for every parameter. The ternary weight is recomputed from the latent one on every forward pass.

blocks.title: Forward quantizer vs the gradient STE pretends it has

scenes.caption: Forward pass: the latent weight is snapped to -gamma, 0 or +gamma. The flat steps have zero slope, so the true gradient is useless.
Backward pass: STE treats the staircase as the line y = w, slope 1, so the loss gradient reaches the latent weight unchanged.
gamma is recomputed from the weights each step. A smaller gamma narrows the zero band (|w| < gamma / 2) and lowers the step height.

blocks.md: The official training code implements STE with a one-line trick. `w + (q(w) - w).detach()` evaluates to `q(w)` in the forward pass, but `detach()` hides the difference from autograd (PyTorch's automatic differentiation), so the gradient with respect to `w` is exactly 1.

blocks.code:
def weight_quant(w):
    scale = 1.0 / w.abs().mean().clamp_(min=1e-5)
    return (w * scale).round().clamp_(-1, 1) / scale

def activation_quant(x):
    scale = 127.0 / x.abs().max(dim=-1, keepdim=True).values.clamp_(min=1e-5)
    return (x * scale).round().clamp_(-128, 127) / scale

class BitLinear(nn.Linear):          # training version
    def forward(self, x):
        w = self.weight                # latent full-precision weights
        x_norm = RMSNorm(x)
        # straight-through estimator via detach()
        x_quant = x_norm + (activation_quant(x_norm) - x_norm).detach()
        w_quant = w + (weight_quant(w) - w).detach()
        return F.linear(x_quant, w_quant)
blocks.caption: Condensed from the BitNet team's official PyTorch BitLinear (Training Tips, Code and FAQ). Optimizer states (for Adam, two running averages per weight) and latent weights stay in high precision.

blocks.md:
**Should the gradient be gated?** A common STE variant comes from the binarized neural networks of Courbariaux, Hubara and colleagues (2016): pass the gradient only where the input lies inside the quantizer's range ($|r| \le 1$) and cancel it outside. That paper also clips latent weights to [-1, 1] after each update, because otherwise they 'would grow very large without any impact on the binary weights'.

BitNet's official code does neither. The `detach()` trick gives slope 1 everywhere, even for a latent weight at 3 gamma, far past 1.5 gamma where RoundClip starts clipping. The papers do not explain the choice, but the setup differs: gamma is the mean of |w| over the matrix, so a latent weight that grows does change the forward pass through the shared scale, and weight decay in stage 1 keeps magnitudes in check. For your own BitLinear, start from the ungated version the published recipe was tuned with.

nodes.label:
Ship: ternary W
plus one gamma

scenes.caption: Every step starts from the latent weights, which accumulate tiny updates in high precision.
Forward: ternarize on the fly and run the network exactly as it will run at inference.
Backward: the gradient passes straight through the quantizer and the optimizer updates the latent weights.
After training the latent weights are discarded. Only the ternary values and the per-matrix scale ship; they are what the network was trained with.

blocks.md: A latent weight can move for many steps without its ternary value changing. Here is a simplified trace: one latent weight starting at 0.30, a gradient that nudges it down by 0.03 per step, and gamma held fixed at 0.5 (in reality gamma drifts as all weights move).

blocks.title: A latent weight drifting until its ternary value flips

scenes.caption: Start: 0.30 / 0.5 = 0.60 rounds to +1.
One update later the latent weight is 0.27 (ratio 0.54). The ternary weight is still +1: the forward pass saw no change at all.
At 0.24 the ratio 0.48 drops below 0.5 and the weight flips to 0. Only now does the model's behavior change.
It stays 0 until the latent weight falls below -0.25. The magnitude of the latent weight acts like a confidence score for the ternary value.

blocks.md:
That picture explains the training recipe the BitNet team reports:

- **Large learning rate.** Small updates often change no ternary weight, so the original BitNet found a larger learning rate the simplest fix; BitNet trained stably at learning rates where the FP16 Transformer diverged. For b1.58 at 700M they used a peak of 1.5e-3 versus 2.5e-4 for the LLaMA baseline.
- **Two-stage schedule.** Decay the learning rate abruptly midway; the loss drops sharply there. Their 1-bit loss curves are S-shaped, so early checkpoints underpredict the final result.
- **Weight decay 0.1, then 0.** Weight decay shrinks latent weights (each step subtracts learning rate times 0.1 times w from every weight w), lowering their confidence and making ternary values flip more often, so it is switched off in the second stage.

Training a BitNet is not cheaper than training an FP16 model with today's code. Latent weights, gradients and optimizer states are high precision, and the FAQ notes their training ran in FP16/BF16 with no speedup. The savings are at inference.

This is the difference between **quantization-aware training from scratch** (training with the quantizer inside the forward pass) and **post-training quantization**. The FAQ adds that they tried continuing training from a 1-bit PTQ checkpoint and saw no improvement over training from scratch. The 2B4T report shows the payoff at 2B scale against INT4 (4-bit integer) PTQ of a strong model, Qwen2.5 1.5B from Alibaba's Qwen team. Its score averages three benchmarks: **MMLU** (Massive Multitask Language Understanding, multiple-choice questions across 57 subjects), **GSM8K** (Grade School Math 8K, about 8,500 grade-school math word problems) and **IFEval** (Instruction-Following Eval, prompts with checkable instructions such as a minimum word count).

blocks.question: Halfway through training, the BitNet b1.58 recipe sets weight decay to 0. Why does that help a ternary model in particular?
options: Weight decay is incompatible with the STE gradient
Weight decay shrinks latent weights toward the rounding threshold, so ternary values keep flipping; removing it lets them settle
Weight decay would push ternary values toward 2
It saves optimizer memory
blocks.explain: The latent weight's magnitude acts as confidence in its ternary value. Decay keeps pulling magnitudes down toward the |w| < gamma/2 band, causing frequent flips. With decay off and a lower learning rate, the ternary weights can converge.

blocks.question: What does the straight-through estimator do in BitLinear?
options: It computes the exact gradient of RoundClip
It quantizes the gradients to ternary values
It skips the quantizer in the forward pass during training
It uses the quantized weights in the forward pass and treats the quantizer as identity in the backward pass
blocks.explain: Forward uses w_quant so the loss reflects the ternary network; the detach() trick makes d(w_quant)/dw equal to 1, so gradients flow to the latent weights. The exact gradient of rounding is zero almost everywhere, and gradients stay high precision.

lessons.title: Does ternary scale? The evidence and its limits

blocks.md: Lesson 1 summed up the b1.58 paper in one line: ternary matches FP16 from 3B parameters up. Before you build on that, look at what was measured. The b1.58 team trained ternary models and their own FP16 LLaMA-style baselines at 700M, 1.3B and 3B parameters, every one on the same 100 billion tokens of RedPajama (an open web-text dataset), plus a 3.9B ternary model. Here is validation perplexity (lower is better) from the paper's Table 1.

blocks.title: Validation perplexity, LLaMA FP16 vs b1.58 (b1.58 paper, Table 1)

scenes.caption: At 700M the ternary model is clearly worse: perplexity 12.87 against 12.33 for FP16.
At 1.3B the gap nearly closes: 11.29 against 11.25.
At 3B ternary is slightly ahead: 9.91 against 10.04. This is the 'matches FP16 from 3B' result.
A 3.9B ternary model reaches 9.62 while, per the paper, running 2.4x faster with 3.32x less memory than the 3B FP16 model.

blocks.md:
The zero-shot averages tell the same story: 45.5 vs 44.3 at 700M, 49.7 (LLaMA) vs 50.2 (b1.58) at 3B, and 51.2 for the 3.9B ternary model. The team also trained a 3B ternary model on 2 trillion tokens with the data recipe of StableLM-3B and beat it on five tasks (average 74.34 vs 73.22).

The 7B, 13B and 70B numbers in the paper are cost measurements: at 70B, 4.1x faster decoding, 7.16x less memory and 41.2x less estimated end-to-end energy than the FP16 model. The paper reports no accuracy for ternary models above 3.9B.

Read the scale. The accuracy evidence in the b1.58 paper stops at 3.9B parameters and 100B tokens, plus one 3B model at 2T tokens. Everything larger is a measurement of speed, memory and energy, not of quality.

blocks.prompt: Spectra (Kaushal et al., 2024), an independent group, trained ternary TriLMs and FP16 FloatLMs from 99M to 3.9B parameters on the same 300B tokens. Does the 3.9B ternary model match the 3.9B FP16 model everywhere?
blocks.reveal: **On benchmarks, yes; on perplexity, not quite.** TriLM 3.9B matches FloatLM 3.9B across their commonsense, reasoning and knowledge benchmarks (including MMLU and TriviaQA), while being 5.9x smaller in bits. But its validation perplexity stays higher on web corpora (a SlimPajama test split, Dolma, C4, RefinedWeb), and it shows the same toxicity and stereotyping as FloatLM 3.9B. Measured in bits, TriLM 3.9B reaches the validation loss of FloatLM 1.1B, which is about 1.7x larger in bits.

blocks.md: Spectra also fit a scaling law to the final validation losses. The form is the one from Chinchilla (Hoffmann et al., 2022, DeepMind's compute-optimal scaling study): loss falls as a power of the parameter count $N$ toward an offset $\epsilon$ that more parameters cannot remove. All runs used 300B tokens, so the fit holds data fixed.

blocks.caption: Both families share the exponent 0.26, so they improve at the same rate with size; TriLM starts higher (A) and levels off higher (epsilon).

blocks.title: Spectra's fitted loss vs parameters (300B tokens)

scenes.caption: At 99M parameters the fits give 3.30 (ternary) and 3.00 (FP16): ternary is about 10% worse.
At 3.9B, the largest size trained, 2.35 and 2.18: the gap has shrunk to about 8% of the FP16 loss.
Right of the line is extrapolation. The gap keeps shrinking, which the authors read as near parity at scale, but as fitted it never closes: it tends to the offset difference, 1.76 - 1.67 = 0.09.

blocks.md:
**ParetoQ** (Liu et al., Meta, 2025) asks the question a deployer cares about: for a fixed number of bytes, which bit width gives the best model? It trains 1, 1.58, 2, 3 and 4-bit models with one framework, tuning the training schedule and quantizer for each, and compares them on accuracy against model size. Its findings:

- Ternary, 2-bit and 3-bit models tie on the size-accuracy Pareto frontier (the curve of best accuracy for each size) and generally beat 4-bit and binary.
- There is a sharp change between 2 and 3 bits: at 3 bits and above, quantization-aware fine-tuning stays close to the pretrained weights; at 2 bits and below the representations change drastically.
- With a fixed budget of 100B tokens, spending about 90% on full-precision pretraining and 10% on quantization-aware fine-tuning beat quantization-aware training from scratch, unlike what the BitNet team reported for its own setup (lesson 4).
- The tiebreaker is hardware: 2-bit is easier to make fast than ternary or 3-bit.

A third line of work warns that low precision gets harder the longer you train. **Scaling Laws for Precision** (Kumar et al., 2024), fit on 465 pretraining runs, finds that the damage from post-training quantization grows with the number of training tokens, to the point where more pretraining data can make the quantized model worse. **Low-Bit Quantization Favors Undertrained LLMs** (Ouyang et al., 2024) measured this on over 1,500 quantized Pythia checkpoints and fit a law for the quantization-induced degradation (QiD), the loss increase after GPTQ, in terms of parameters $N$, training tokens $D$ and bits $P$.

blocks.caption: More tokens raise the damage, more parameters and more bits lower it. Fit on Pythia checkpoints up to 12B parameters and about 206B training tokens with GPTQ; values far beyond that are the paper's extrapolation.

blocks.title: Fitted loss increase from GPTQ vs training tokens

scenes.caption: A 7B model: 3-bit GPTQ adds about 0.14 to the loss (cross-entropy in nats) at 100B training tokens, 0.48 at 1T and 2.0 at 15T. Every curve rises with data.
At 70B the same curves sit lower (3-bit: 0.29 at 1T tokens). Bigger models tolerate quantization better.
At 1B they sit higher (3-bit: 0.75 at 1T). Small, heavily trained models are the hard case for low-bit PTQ.

blocks.md:
That law is about post-training quantization, but the same paper replicated BitNet b1.58 at 120M and 1.2B parameters against BF16 twins. Early in training BitNet matched or beat BF16 (helped by its larger learning rate); later the 120M BitNet fell behind, and a gap opened at 1.2B too. The authors read this as native low-bit models also favoring undertrained regimes, with the gap appearing later than for PTQ, and note that BitNet results at the time used at most 100B tokens.

2B4T is the counterpoint in that regime: 4 trillion tokens for 2 billion parameters, 2,000 tokens per parameter, and still within about one point of Qwen2.5 1.5B on the report's benchmark average (54.19 vs 55.23, lesson 7).

Ternary trained from scratch tracks FP16 closely from a few billion parameters, and beats 4-bit PTQ per byte. The open questions are scale (little quality evidence above 4B parameters) and data: more tokens per parameter makes every low-precision format work harder.

blocks.question: Under Ouyang et al.'s fitted law, which checkpoint loses the most loss from 3-bit GPTQ?
options: A 70B model trained on 100B tokens
A 1B model trained on 1T tokens
A 70B model trained on 1T tokens
All three lose the same, since only bit width matters
blocks.explain: The law gives about 0.75 for 1B at 1T tokens, 0.29 for 70B at 1T and 0.085 for 70B at 100B. Damage grows with tokens (exponent 0.53) and shrinks with size (exponent 0.23), so the small, heavily trained model suffers most.

blocks.question: ParetoQ compared 1, 1.58, 2, 3 and 4-bit models under one framework. Which conclusion does it report?
options: Ternary, 2-bit and 3-bit tie on accuracy per size and generally beat 4-bit and binary; 2-bit is the most hardware-friendly
4-bit is always on the Pareto frontier and lower bit widths never pay off
Binary weights give the best accuracy per byte
Only training from scratch works below 3 bits
blocks.explain: ParetoQ finds the three middle widths tied and ahead of 4-bit and binary, with kernels as the tiebreaker. It also found fine-tuning a full-precision model (about 10% of the budget) beat quantization-aware training from scratch, and binary lagged clearly.

lessons.title: The full 2B4T recipe, then BitNet v2 and BitNet Distillation

blocks.md:
BitLinear makes 2B4T ternary, but it is not the whole model. The report and the released GPU code describe the rest of each layer:

- **Pre-norm plus subLN.** An RMSNorm before attention and before the FFN, as in LLaMA, plus an extra RMSNorm (subLN) right before the attention output and FFN down projections. Every BitLinear input is still normalized (lesson 3), but Q, K and V share one norm, as do gate and up.
- **Squared ReLU.** The FFN keeps its gate, up and down matrices (lesson 1) but swaps SwiGLU's gate, SiLU(x) = x sigmoid(x), for $\mathrm{ReLU}^2(x) = \max(0, x)^2$: -1.5 gives 0, 0.5 gives 0.25, 2 gives 4. The report chose it to raise sparsity: every negative input becomes an exact 0.
- **RoPE** (rotary position embeddings): each pair of query and key coordinates is rotated by an angle proportional to the token's position, so attention scores depend on relative position.
- **No bias terms**, and the **LLaMA 3 tokenizer**: byte-pair encoding (merge frequent byte pairs into tokens) with the 128,256-token vocabulary of lesson 1.

blocks.title: One 2B4T layer (from the released GPU model code)

scenes.caption: Attention half: pre-norm, then the Q, K and V BitLinears, RoPE and attention. Attention itself multiplies activations by activations, so it is not ternary.
subLN normalizes the attention output before the O projection, keeping the variance of what gets quantized stable. Then the residual add.
FFN half: gate and up BitLinears, ReLU^2 on the gate times up, subLN, then the down BitLinear. Its output is added to the residual stream the same way.
Ternary parts: 7 matrices per layer (Q, K, V, O, gate, up, down), the 69,468,160 weights of lesson 1. Norms, RoPE, attention math and the embedding stay in higher precision.

blocks.md:
The training pipeline has three phases, and the 1-bit choices show up in each:

1. **Pretraining, stage 1** (about the first half of 4T tokens): cosine learning-rate decay from a relatively high peak, because 1-bit models train more stably; weight decay on a cosine schedule peaking at 0.1; mostly general web data such as DCLM and FineWeb-EDU (the corpus also includes synthetic math data).
2. **Pretraining, stage 2 (cooldown)**: the learning rate drops abruptly, then follows a cosine from a much lower peak; weight decay is 0; higher-quality curated data.
3. **Supervised fine-tuning (SFT)** on public instruction and chat datasets plus synthetic data, then **DPO** (direct preference optimization, which trains on pairs of preferred and rejected answers without a separate reward model) for 2 epochs at learning rate 2e-7 with beta 0.1 on UltraFeedback and MagPie. No reinforcement learning was used.

blocks.title: 2B4T training pipeline (schematic, not to scale)

scenes.caption: Stage 1: high peak learning rate with cosine decay, weight decay up to 0.1, general web data. Pretraining is 4T tokens and dwarfs the later phases; widths here are not to scale.

Stage 2 starts about midway through the tokens: the learning rate drops abruptly, weight decay goes to 0, and curated data takes over. Lesson 4's latent-weight picture explains why decay is switched off.
SFT on chat and instruction data, with a summed loss, a larger learning rate and more epochs than usual for full precision. Then DPO on preference pairs: 2 epochs, learning rate 2e-7, beta 0.1.

blocks.prompt: In SFT the 2B4T team changed how the loss over a batch is combined, and moved the learning rate relative to typical full-precision fine-tuning. Which way do you think the learning rate went?
blocks.reveal: **Up.** The report says the 1-bit model benefited from a relatively larger SFT learning rate and needed more epochs, consistent with its pretraining. The loss change: they **summed** the per-token cross-entropy over the batch instead of averaging it, which they found converged better. Both fit lesson 4's picture: a ternary weight only changes when its latent value crosses a threshold, so small updates do nothing.

blocks.md:
**BitNet v2** (Wang, Ma, Wei, 2025) attacks the 8-bit activations. With weights at 1.58 bits, the matmul still runs on INT8 inputs, while new GPUs offer native 4-bit math that batched inference could use. The obstacle is outliers: the inputs to the QKV and up/gate projections are roughly Gaussian, but the inputs to the attention output projection and the FFN down projection have outlier channels.

The fix is **H-BitLinear** for those two projections only: apply a **Hadamard transform** to the normalized activations before quantizing. A Hadamard matrix has entries of plus or minus one over $\sqrt{n}$ with orthogonal rows, so it is a rotation: it preserves lengths and spreads one large entry across all coordinates. It runs in $O(n \log n)$ with a fast transform. The model trains with the rotation in place, so its weights simply live in the rotated coordinates.

blocks.tex: H_m = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{pmatrix} H_{m-1} & H_{m-1} \\ H_{m-1} & -H_{m-1} \end{pmatrix},\ H_0 = (1); \qquad Q_{\mathrm{INT4}}(X) = \frac{\beta}{\sqrt{7}}\,\mathrm{RoundClip}\!\left(\frac{\sqrt{7}}{\beta+\epsilon}X, -8, 7\right),\ \beta = \mathrm{mean}(|X|)
blocks.caption: Left: the recursive Hadamard matrix for n = 2^m. Right: BitNet v2's 4-bit activation quantizer, per token, which uses the mean absolute value rather than the max.

blocks.title: Why rotate before 4-bit quantization (8 values, BitNet v2's INT4 rule)

scenes.caption: One token with an outlier channel: 6.0 at index 2, the rest small. Its mean absolute value beta is 0.9125.
Quantize directly: the scale sqrt(7)/beta = 2.90 sends 6.0 to 17.4, clipped to 7. Dequantized, 6.0 becomes 2.41. Root-mean-square error over the 8 values: 1.27.
Rotate first with the 8 x 8 Hadamard matrix. Same length, but the outlier is spread over all 8 coordinates: every entry is now between 1.66 and 2.44 in size.
Quantize the rotated vector, then rotate back to compare: error 0.24, over 5x lower than 1.27. Nothing was clipped.

blocks.md: BitNet v2 trains from scratch with 8-bit activations, then continues training briefly with 4-bit activations in all linear layers. On 100B tokens of RedPajama at 7B parameters, the average over six zero-shot tasks was 58.12 for BitNet b1.58, 58.73 for v2 with 8-bit activations and 58.30 for v2 with 4-bit activations (perplexity 9.09, 9.14 and 9.24); BitNet a4.8 scored 57.91.

**BitNet Distillation** (BitDistill; Wu et al., 2025) attacks the other cost: pretraining from scratch on trillions of tokens. It turns an existing full-precision model into a 1.58-bit model *for one downstream task*, in three stages:

1. **Modeling refinement**: insert subLN before the attention output and FFN down projections, as in BitNet, to stabilize the quantized model.
2. **Continued pretraining** of the ternary model on 10B tokens of general text (versus about 4T for 2B4T from scratch).
3. **Distillation-based fine-tuning** on the task, with the fine-tuned FP16 model as teacher: a logits distillation loss (the student matches the teacher's output distribution) plus MiniLM-style attention-relation distillation on one layer (the student matches the teacher's patterns of similarity between queries, keys and values).

blocks.title: MNLI accuracy from Qwen3 bases (BitNet Distillation, Table 1)

scenes.caption: Full-precision fine-tuning on MNLI, a sentence-pair inference task: 88.01, 89.61 and 91.48 at 0.6B, 1.7B and 4B.
Ternarize the model and fine-tune directly: 74.09, 75.27, 76.11. The gap grows with size, from about 14 to over 15 points: direct conversion does not scale.

BitDistill: 88.17, 89.53, 91.40, matching FP16 at every size. On a CPU with 16 threads the paper's single speed figure is 1,135 tokens/s against 427, in 0.11 GB against 1.20 GB (sizes that fit the 0.6B model).

blocks.md: BitDistill produces task-specific models (classification and summarization in the paper), not a general chat model. For a general-purpose ternary model, the strongest published result is still native pretraining (2B4T). General conversions exist (ParetoQ's short quantization-aware phase, lesson 5; a 1.58-bit Llama 3 8B fine-tuned on 100B tokens), but the converted Llama 3 8B still trailed the original.

blocks.question: A team has a strong 7B FP16 model and needs a ternary model for one text-classification task, with budget for about 10B extra training tokens. Which plan does the published evidence support best?
options: Pretrain a 7B ternary model from scratch on the 10B tokens
Ternarize the weights with absmean and fine-tune on the task directly
Insert subLN, continue pretraining the ternary model on the 10B tokens, then fine-tune on the task while distilling from the FP16 model
Post-training quantize to ternary with GPTQ and skip training
blocks.explain: That is BitDistill, which matched FP16 fine-tuning on MNLI at 0.6B to 4B. Direct ternary fine-tuning lost 14 to 15 points, 10B tokens are far too few for pretraining from scratch (2B4T used 4T), and PTQ to so few bits collapses (lesson 1 at 1 and 2 bits; lesson 8 for ternary).

blocks.question: Why does BitNet v2 put the Hadamard transform only before the attention output and FFN down projections?
options: Those two matrices are the only ternary ones
The Hadamard transform only works on square matrices
They are the largest matrices, so the rotation saves the most memory
Their inputs, the intermediate states, have outlier channels, while the inputs to the QKV and up/gate projections are already roughly Gaussian
blocks.explain: The paper measured the activation distributions: intermediate states have outlier channels and many near-zero entries, which wreck 4-bit quantization. The other inputs are Gaussian-like already, so they need no rotation. All seven projections are ternary, and the rotation saves no memory; it reduces quantization error.

lessons.title: Running ternary models fast: I2_S, lookup tables, real numbers

blocks.md: No CPU or GPU has a native ternary type, so packing and the kernel decide whether the theory turns into speed. The 2B4T GPU kernel stores **four ternary values in one int8** in HBM, loads them into shared memory, unpacks and computes ('pack-store-load-unpack-compute'). On CPUs, **bitnet.cpp** (built on llama.cpp, the widely used open-source C/C++ program for running language models on CPUs) offers three kernels.

**I2_S** (Int2 with a Scale: 2-bit integer codes plus the weight scale) maps each weight to a 2-bit code offline: -1 to `00`, 0 to `01`, +1 to `10`. At run time it unpacks and does an ordinary multiply-then-add with the INT8 activations. Simple, 2 bits per weight, and the paper recommends it with enough threads.

blocks.title: I2_S: four ternary weights become one byte

scenes.caption: Row 0 of our toy matrix: four ternary weights.
Each weight gets a 2-bit code: +1 is 10, 0 is 01, -1 is 00. Code 11 is never used, which is why 2 bits per weight wastes about 0.4 bits.

Four codes fill one byte. Simplified: the real layout interleaves codes across rows to suit SIMD (one instruction, many values) loads. For 2B4T, 2,084,044,800 weights pack into 521,011,200 bytes, matching the U8 tensor size in the released checkpoint.

blocks.md: **TL1 and TL2** remove the multiply-add altogether with lookup tables (TL stands for ternary lookup table; the idea comes from T-MAC, a Microsoft lookup-table kernel library for low-bit models on CPUs, and LUT-GEMM, a lookup-table matrix multiply for quantized language models). For a pair of weights there are only $3^2 = 9$ possible patterns. So for each pair of activations, precompute all 9 signed sums once, then each pair of weights becomes a 4-bit index into that table (3 bits name only 8 patterns).

blocks.caption: In words: shift each weight from -1..1 to 0..2 and read the pair as a two-digit base-3 number; the entry is the signed sum that pair produces. This matches the TL1 table in the bitnet.cpp report: (-1,-1) is index 0 and (+1,+1) is index 8.

blocks.title: TL1: two lookups replace the row-0 dot product

scenes.caption: With x_q = [64, -20, 127, 34], precompute all 9 sums for (x0, x1) = (64, -20). Index 0 is -64 + 20 = -44; index 8 is 64 - 20 = 44. This is done once per token and reused by every output row.
Same for (x2, x3) = (127, 34). Now each output row needs no arithmetic per weight, only lookups and adds.
Row 0 weights (+1, 0) give index 3 x 2 + 1 = 7: look up 64.
Weights (+1, -1) give index 3 x 2 + 0 = 6: look up 93. 64 + 93 = 157, the same integer sum as the add/subtract loop, with one lookup-and-add per weight pair instead of one operation per weight.

blocks.md: **TL2** groups three weights: 27 patterns. Half of them are negatives of the other half (the pattern (-1,0,1) gives minus the sum of (1,0,-1)), so the table only needs 14 entries (13 mirror pairs plus all zeros) and a separate **sign bit** says whether to negate. Three weights then cost a 4-bit index plus 1 sign bit: 5 bits for 3 weights, **1.67 bits per weight**, which the report says shrinks the model by 1/6 compared with TL1. The 14 entries fit a 16-entry SIMD shuffle (16 x int8 = 128 bits for AVX2 `vpshufb`), which is why groups of 3 is the limit. AVX2 (Advanced Vector Extensions 2) is the x86 vector instruction set, and `vpshufb` treats 16 bytes as a table and looks up many 4-bit indexes in one instruction. Groups of 4 would give 81 patterns, 41 entries even after mirroring, which do not fit.

blocks.title: Memory for 2B4T's 2.08B linear weights by format

scenes.caption: Computed from the config: 2,084,044,800 weights x bits / 8. FP16 is 4.17 GB, INT4 1.04 GB.
2-bit packing gives 0.52 GB, TL2 0.43 GB, and the information limit 0.41 GB. The report quotes 0.4 GB of non-embedding memory.

Now the surprise: the 128,256 x 2560 embedding in BF16 is 0.66 GB, bigger than every ternary weight combined. Total parameters are about 2.41B, which is why the bitnet.cpp README lists the model as 2.4B.

blocks.md:
Reported results (measured by the authors, not re-run here):

- **2B4T vs similar open models** (2B4T report, Table 1): 0.4 GB non-embedding memory vs 2.6 GB for Qwen2.5 1.5B; CPU decode latency 29 ms per token vs 65 ms; estimated decode energy 0.028 J vs 0.347 J; average benchmark score 54.19 vs 55.23.
- **b1.58 on GPU** (2024 paper, 2-bit kernel from Ladder, a Microsoft Research compiler for low-precision kernels): at 3B, 2.71x faster decoding and 3.55x less memory than LLaMA 3B; at 70B on two NVIDIA A100 data-center GPUs, 11x the batch size and 8.9x the throughput.
- **bitnet.cpp vs llama.cpp FP16** (CPU report, on test models of various sizes): 1.37x to 5.07x faster on an Apple M2 Ultra, 2.37x to 6.17x on an Intel i7-13700H, 55.4% to 82.2% less energy, and a 100B ternary model at 5 to 7 tokens per second on one CPU.

**The GPU kernel up close.** The 2B4T kernel in the microsoft/BitNet repository is a W2A8 **GEMV**, a matrix-vector product for one token at a time, with 2-bit weights and 8-bit activations. Offline, the converter adds 2 to every ternary weight, so -1, 0 and +1 become the 2-bit codes 01, 10 and 11 (a different code from bitnet.cpp's I2_S). It cuts each matrix into 16 x 32 blocks, permutes each block so the values one GPU thread needs sit together, and packs 16 codes into each 32-bit word in an interleaved order. Follow one word below.

blocks.title: W2A8 GPU kernel: 16 weights in one 32-bit word

scenes.caption: Sixteen ternary weights of one row piece. The first four are row 0 of our toy matrix. Each is stored as weight + 2: codes 01, 10 or 11.
The 2-bit slots of the word, lowest bits first, hold w0, w4, w8, w12, w1, w5, ... This is the interleaving order [0, 4, 8, 12, 1, 5, 9, 13, ...] listed in the repository README.
Why: slots 0, 4, 8 and 12 are the lowest 2 bits of the word's four bytes. One AND with 0x03030303 pulls w0 to w3 into four bytes at once; subtracting 2 from each byte gives -1, 0, +1 as int8.

dp4a multiplies four int8 pairs and adds them into a 32-bit integer in one instruction: 64 + 0 + 127 - 34 = 157, row 0's sum from lesson 3. Shifting the word by 2, 4 and 6 bits yields w4 to w15 the same way.

blocks.md: The README's A100 40GB measurements (not run here): 13.32 microseconds against 18.32 for BF16 on a 2560 x 2560 matrix (1.38x), 14.49 against 37.78 on 2560 x 6912 (2.61x) and 30.99 against 112.39 on 20480 x 3200 (3.63x). The bytes shrink 8x, so why not 8x faster? At the A100 40GB's 1,555 GB/s, the 1.64 MB of packed 2560 x 2560 weights take about 1.05 microseconds to read, so the measured 13.32 is mostly fixed costs. Even the largest shape, 20480 x 3200, would read its 16.4 MB in about 10.5 microseconds at full bandwidth, a third of the measured 30.99; BF16 there reaches about three quarters of it (84 of 112 microseconds). End to end, the README reports 2B4T with this kernel about 3x faster than BF16 Gemma-2-2B in vLLM.

**Why batch size changes the picture.** A GEMV uses each weight byte once, so it is memory-bound and fewer bytes means more speed. With B tokens in a batch each weight read serves B tokens, and past the roofline's ridge point the step becomes math-bound (GPU and inference basics). Then bytes stop mattering, and since the kernel unpacks ternary weights into ordinary int8 values, the arithmetic is plain INT8: a ternary model can at best match an INT8 model. This is why the 2B4T report says commodity GPUs are not designed for 1-bit models and calls for dedicated low-bit logic. The b1.58 paper's 8.9x throughput at 70B came from memory capacity: smaller weights left room for 11x the batch size.

bitnet.cpp's kernels are **lossless**: they reproduce the training-time quantization exactly. On 1,000 prompts with a 700M BitNet b1.58 model, I2_S, TL1 and TL2 produced exactly the same output tokens (up to 100 per prompt) as an FP32 kernel 100% of the time, versus 1.4% for llama.cpp's own ternary formats TQ1_0 and TQ2_0, which quantize activations in 256-element blocks unlike training.

Loading the 2B4T checkpoint in Hugging Face `transformers` (the standard Python model library) saves memory but gives no speed or energy gain; the model card says the efficiency needs the dedicated bitnet.cpp kernels.

Tradeoffs and open problems:

- **Pretraining is the strongest path.** The best general ternary model, 2B4T, was trained from scratch. Converting a full-precision model also works with a long enough quantization-aware phase (ParetoQ, lesson 5; a Llama 3 8B fine-tuned on 100B tokens still trailed the original); BitNet Distillation (lesson 6) needs only 10B tokens but gives single-task models.
- **Activations are still 8-bit.** BitNet a4.8 (named for 4-bit activations, with 8-bit for sparsified states) pushes inputs to attention and FFN to 4 bits and sparsifies intermediate states, activating 55% of parameters and supporting a 3-bit KV cache; BitNet v2 reaches native 4-bit activations with a Hadamard rotation (lesson 6).
- **Not everything is ternary.** Embeddings, the output head, norms and attention math stay higher precision.
- **Hardware.** The 2B4T report notes commodity GPUs are not designed for 1-bit models and calls for hardware co-design.
- **Scale.** 2B4T has 2B parameters and a 4,096-token context; the report lists larger models and longer context as future work.

blocks.question: Why can TL2 store three ternary weights in 5 bits while TL1 needs 4 bits for two?
options: TL2 uses 5 bits per weight
TL2 compresses the activations instead of the weights
TL2 uses mirror symmetry: 27 patterns become 14 unsigned table entries plus a 1-bit sign, so a 4-bit index plus a sign bit covers three weights
TL2 drops the zero value
blocks.explain: Negating all three weights negates the sum, so only half the patterns need table entries (14, including all zeros). A 4-bit index picks the entry and a sign bit flips it. 5 bits / 3 weights = 1.67 bits per weight, versus 4/2 = 2 for TL1.

blocks.question: After packing 2B4T's linear weights into 2 bits, which part of the model is now the largest single block of weights?
options: The attention Q and K projections
The BF16 embedding and tied output head, about 0.66 GB
The FFN weights, still 2.08 GB
The RMSNorm parameters
blocks.explain: The 128,256 x 2560 embedding is 328M parameters at 2 bytes: 0.66 GB, versus 0.52 GB for all 2.08B ternary weights. Because the embeddings are tied, the output head reads that matrix every token, which is why large vocabularies matter more once the rest is ternary.

blocks.question: A ternary model runs on an A100 at batch 512 with this style of kernel (unpack to int8, then int8 dot products). Compared with the same model stored as plain INT8 weights, what speedup should you expect at this batch size?
options: Little or none: the step is math-bound, and the ternary kernel still does INT8 arithmetic, so at best it matches INT8
About 4x, because 2-bit weights are 4x smaller than INT8
About 8x, from the 16-to-2-bit ratio
A slowdown of exactly 4x from unpacking
blocks.explain: At large batch the weight bytes are amortized over many tokens, so the step is limited by arithmetic, and both versions end up multiplying int8 values. Unpacking adds some work but not a fixed 4x. The byte savings still help memory capacity, which allows larger batches or longer contexts.

lessons.title: Build it yourself: train a tiny BitNet and run it from packed bytes

blocks.md: Time to run the whole pipeline yourself, small enough for a laptop CPU: train, export, pack, and run from packed bytes. The model is a character-level GPT on Tiny Shakespeare: 2 layers, width 128, 4 heads, a gated ReLU^2 FFN of width 256 (2B4T's FFN in miniature), 64 characters of context. Its 14 linear layers hold **327,680 weights**; the embeddings, positions, norm gains and output head (27,008 more parameters) stay full precision, as in 2B4T. Every number below comes from one run on an Apple Silicon laptop CPU with PyTorch limited to 2 threads.

blocks.code:
class BitLinear(nn.Linear):                  # nn.Linear plus its own RMSNorm
    def __init__(self, i, o):
        super().__init__(i, o, bias=False)
        self.norm, self.quant = nn.RMSNorm(i, eps=1e-5), True
    def forward(self, x):
        x = self.norm(x)
        if not self.quant:                      # FP32 twin: same architecture
            return F.linear(x, self.weight)
        xq = x + (activation_quant(x) - x).detach()      # STE, lesson 4
        wq = self.weight + (weight_quant(self.weight) - self.weight).detach()
        return F.linear(xq, wq)

class Block(nn.Module):                         # D=128, H=4, FF=256
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.q, self.k, self.v, self.o = (BitLinear(D, D) for _ in range(4))
        self.gate, self.up = BitLinear(D, FF), BitLinear(D, FF)
        self.down = BitLinear(FF, D)
    def forward(self, x):
        b, t, _ = x.shape
        sh = lambda z: z.view(b, t, H, D // H).transpose(1, 2)
        a = F.scaled_dot_product_attention(sh(self.q(x)), sh(self.k(x)),
                                           sh(self.v(x)), is_causal=True)
        x = x + self.o(a.transpose(1, 2).reshape(b, t, D))
        return x + self.down(F.relu(self.gate(x)) ** 2 * self.up(x))
blocks.caption: The swap. weight_quant and activation_quant are the official functions from lesson 4. With quant False the same model is an ordinary FP32 network, so the two runs differ only in the quantizer.

blocks.md: The experiment: same seed, same batches, same schedule (100 warmup steps, cosine decay to 10% of the peak), AdamW with weight decay 0.1, 3,000 steps of 32 sequences. Train the FP32 twin and the ternary model at three peak learning rates each: 1e-3, 4e-3 and 1.6e-2. Then take the best FP32 model and post-training quantize it: switch its BitLinears to ternary weights and INT8 activations without any further training. The bars show validation loss (cross-entropy in nats per character; an untrained model scores about 4.4).

blocks.reveal: **Much worse: 2.888.** Training with the quantizer in the loop found ternary weights that work (1.657); rounding weights that were optimized as real numbers loses most of what the model learned. This is lesson 1's PTQ collapse, reproduced on a laptop.

blocks.md:
What the run shows, and what it does not:

- **Higher learning rate helps ternary more.** From 1e-3 to 4e-3, ternary improves by 0.15 and FP32 by 0.09. At 1.6e-2 FP32 already gets worse while ternary still improves. This matches the BitNet recipe of lesson 4, on a model thousands of times smaller.
- **A gap remains.** At their best rates ternary is 0.07 nats behind FP32. The b1.58 results say the gap closes only at billions of parameters, so expect it at this size.
- **The value mix drifts to thirds.** At initialization 25% of weights round to 0 (PyTorch initializes linear weights uniformly, and a quarter of a uniform distribution lies within half its mean absolute value of zero). After training at 1.6e-2: 32.5% -1, 35.1% 0, 32.4% +1, the nearly uniform mix the BitNet FAQ reports.

**Export.** Drop the latent weights. For each of the 14 matrices keep only the ternary values and one gamma, and pack 4 weights per byte with I2_S's codes (-1 to 00, 0 to 01, +1 to 10). Simplified: this keeps weights in plain row order, while bitnet.cpp interleaves them for SIMD loads. The packed weights take **81,920 bytes**, exactly 327,680 x 2 / 8, plus 14 four-byte scales; the FP32 weights took 1,310,720 bytes, 16x more. The first byte of the first query matrix is 00001010 (decimal 10): weights -1, -1, +1, +1.

blocks.title: Unpack one byte and accumulate
blocks.code:
packed = 0b10011000        # one I2_S-style byte: codes 10 01 10 00
xq = [64, -20, 127, 34]     # int8 activations
gamma, s = 0.286875, 48.846
acc = 0
for j in range(4):
    code = (packed >> (6 - 2 * j)) & 0b11
    w = code - 1            # 00:-1  01:0  10:+1
    if w == 1:
        acc += xq[j]
    elif w == -1:
        acc -= xq[j]
y = acc * gamma / s

scenes.caption: The byte holds row 0 of lesson 2's toy matrix, (+1, 0, +1, -1), as codes 10 01 10 00, with lesson 3's activations.
j = 0: shift right by 6 and mask the low 2 bits: code 10, so w = +1. Add 64.
j = 1: shift by 4, code 01, w = 0. Skip: no add, no multiply.
j = 2: shift by 2, code 10, w = +1. Add 127.
j = 3: no shift, code 00, w = -1. Subtract 34. The integer sum is 157, as in lesson 3.
One float multiply for the whole output: 157 x 0.286875 / 48.846 = 0.922.

blocks.code:
def pack(t):            # t: int8 ternary (n, k) -> uint8 (n, k/4)
    c = (t + 1).astype(np.uint8).reshape(t.shape[0], -1, 4)  # -1:00 0:01 +1:10
    return (c[..., 0] << 6) | (c[..., 1] << 4) | (c[..., 2] << 2) | c[..., 3]

def unpack(p):
    c = np.stack([(p >> 6) & 3, (p >> 4) & 3, (p >> 2) & 3, p & 3], axis=-1)
    return c.reshape(p.shape[0], -1).astype(np.int8) - 1

def matvec_addsub(p, xq):              # integer adds and subtracts only
    w = unpack(p)
    return (np.where(w == 1, xq, 0).sum(1, dtype=np.int32)
            - np.where(w == -1, xq, 0).sum(1, dtype=np.int32))

def matvec_tl1(idx, xq):               # idx: one 0..8 index per weight pair
    a, b = xq[0::2].astype(np.int32), xq[1::2].astype(np.int32)
    lut = np.stack([wa * a + wb * b for wa in (-1, 0, 1)
                    for wb in (-1, 0, 1)], axis=1)      # 9 sums per pair
    return lut[np.arange(idx.shape[1]), idx].sum(1, dtype=np.int32)

# y = acc * gamma / s : the one float multiply per output
blocks.caption: The two NumPy kernels: unpack then add and subtract (I2_S style), and TL1-style lookups with 9 precomputed sums per activation pair (lesson 7).

blocks.md:
**Verification.** On random inputs to all 14 layers (each passed through the layer's RMSNorm), both kernels produced exactly the integer sums of an exact integer reference: 0 mismatches. Then every BitLinear in the model was swapped for the packed kernel and the model generated 300 characters greedily, next to the PyTorch forward: **300 of 300 characters identical**.

The logits were not quite identical, though: they differed by up to 0.034. The integer math was exact. The PyTorch forward multiplies dequantized floats, so its layer outputs differ from the integer path in about the seventh significant digit. At one step that tiny difference pushed a single activation in the second block across an INT8 rounding boundary, and the one-level jump spread through the later layers. A pure-PyTorch integer path gives the same 0.034, so NumPy is not the cause. This is what lesson 7's 'lossless' means: identical output tokens, as here, not bit-identical logits. Logits match bit for bit only if both sides quantize the same way with exact integer arithmetic.

**Speed, measured honestly.** On one 6912 x 2560 matrix (2B4T's gate projection shape) with one token: FP32 through BLAS (the tuned linear-algebra library NumPy calls for matrix products) took about 0.5 ms; NumPy unpack-and-add about 20 ms; NumPy TL1 about 30 ms, all with identical integer results. The packed data is 16x smaller (4.42 MB against 70.8 MB), yet NumPy is slower, because each call writes out the unpacked matrix and its temporaries to memory, moving more bytes than the float version reads. The speed of lesson 7 needs kernels that unpack inside registers with SIMD instructions, which is what bitnet.cpp provides.

blocks.md: The whole method fits on a laptop: a quantizer in the forward pass, an STE in the backward pass, then 2 bits per weight and integer adds at inference. The hard part in practice is the kernel, and matching training's quantizers exactly.

blocks.question: Your tiny model's 327,680 ternary weights pack into 81,920 bytes at 2 bits each. Roughly how many bytes would TL2's layout (5 bits per 3 weights) need for the same weights?
options: About 68 KB
About 61 KB
About 82 KB, the same as 2 bits
About 41 KB
blocks.explain: 327,680 x 5 / 3 / 8 is about 68,300 bytes. The log2(3) information limit would be about 64,900 bytes; 41 KB would be 1 bit per weight, which cannot hold three values.

blocks.question: Both NumPy kernels matched the exact integer sums, and an exact integer path written in PyTorch showed the same gap, yet both differed from the PyTorch fake-quant forward by up to 0.034. What does that show?
options: The weights were packed in the wrong order
A float simulation of the quantizer can land on the other side of an INT8 rounding boundary than the integer path, and one flipped activation spreads through later layers
Integer addition in NumPy is inexact
Greedy decoding hides every error, so exactness never matters
blocks.explain: The integer products were exact. The fake-quant forward computes in floats, which differ from the integer path in the last digits; at one step that moved one activation across a rounding boundary and later layers amplified it. bitnet.cpp's lossless result rests on reproducing training's quantization exactly; llama.cpp's TQ formats quantize activations differently and matched only 1.4% of the time.
